The complexity of the internal structure of liposome remains insufﬁciently understood, posing
challenges to the rational design and development of liposomal formulations. In this study, we
employed coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulation to investigate the structural details of the
commercially available nine liposomal formulations, with ﬁve passive loading systems (Arikayce Kit®,
Visudyne®, Ambisome®, Mepact®, and Exparel®) and four active loading systems (Doxil®, Myocet®,
Onivyde®, and Vyxeos®). In ﬁve passive loading liposome systems, protonation of drug molecules
signiﬁcantly reduces their binding to phospholipid membranes and even drastically alters the
morphology and vesicle size in multivesicular liposomes. However, the orientation of drug molecules
in lipid membranes is independent of protonation, with hydrophobic part inward and hydrophilic part
outward. In four active loading systems, the presence of ions within the liposome cavity promotes the
self-aggregation of drugs, thereby enhancing drug retention and release proﬁles. This study provided
valuable molecular insights for marketed liposomes formulation.
Liposomes are self-enclosed, spherical vesicles composed of one or more
phospholipid bilayers. Due to their superior biocompatibility, biodegrad-
ability, as well as their ability to provide controlled release and targeted
delivery, liposomes have been widely utilized in drug delivery and biome-
dicalresearch1. Over the pastthree decades, severalliposomal drug products
have been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and
the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for various medical applications,
but only nine unique products remain available on the current market
(Table 1). Based on the size and internal structure, they can be categorized
into ﬁve distinct types: small unilamellar vesicles (SUVs), large unilamellar
vesicles (LUVs), oligolamellar vesicles (OLVs), multilamellar vesicles
(MLVs), and multivesicular vesicles (MVLs)2–4. Doxil®, Myocet®, and
Ambisome®arecategorizedasSUVstypicallyrangingfrom100to1000 nm,
and theyhave higher biocompatibility and tissue penetration capabilities. In
contrast, Onivyde®, Arikayce Kit®, and Visudyne® are identiﬁed as large
unilamellar vesicles (LUVs) for their increased particle sizes. Vyxeos®
(daunorubicin: cytarabine liposome for injection) is designed as a bilamellar
liposomesystem,whichemergesduringtheinitialloadingofcytarabineinto
the formulation. The process of forming internal layers can be viewed as a
thermodynamic adjustment of the lipid bilayer, aimed at reducing the
surface area-to-volume ratio in response to water loss and external osmotic
conditions5–10. Mepact® is identiﬁed as a multilamellar vesicle (MLVs)
which allows for signiﬁcant encapsulation of lipophilic compounds. The
particle sizes of Mepact® range from 2.0 to 3.5 μm, making them well-suited
for recognition and uptake by monocytes and macrophages. This facilitates
macrophage activation and triggers subsequent immunomodulatory effects
that support cancer treatment11–15. Exparel® (MVLs) is manufactured by
DepoFoam technology, with particle sizes of approximately 10 μm. The
unique honeycomb-like structure within Exparel® encapsulates drugs into
hundreds of cavities, facilitating the gradual release of drugs through the
slow breakdown of liposomes in vivo16–18.
On the other hand, the drug encapsulation process of liposomal for-
mulations can be mainly classiﬁed into two approaches: active and passive
drug loading. Arikayce Kit®, Visudyne®, Ambisome®, Mepact®, and
Exparel® employ a passive drug loading method, which utilizes the spon-
taneous incorporation of the drug into the lipid bilayer during the liposome
formation process. This method simpliﬁes the preparation procedure and
effectively enhances the drug encapsulation efﬁciency and bioavailability.

While Doxil®, Myocet®, Onivyde®, and Vyxeos® employ active drug
loading techniques such as the pH gradient method and ammonium ion
concentration gradient method. Drugs form insoluble complexes within the
liposomes, leading to an increasing concentration gradient between interior
and exterior, which facilitates drug encapsulation. This method enables the
efﬁcient loading of higher drug concentrations into smaller liposomes. For
example, Onivyde® features a particle size of merely 110 nm, with an iri-
notecan concentration within the liposome reaching up to 260 mM.
The diverse and complex structure of liposomes is essential to thor-
oughly understand their properties. Dynamic Light Scattering (DLS) is a
quick, non-invasive method for particle sizing, but it’s sensitive to con-
centration and homogeneity, with limited resolution for complex samples19.
Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) offers high-resolution, non-invasive
molecular analysis without chemical modiﬁcation, but suffers from limited
sensitivity, high cost, and complex data analysis20. Small-angle X-ray scat-
tering (SAXS) is widely used for nanoscale structural analysis of various
materials, but it is limited by complex data interpretation and specialized
equipment21.
Cryo-electron
microscopy
(Cryo-EM)
provides
high-
resolution results in natural states but suffers from complex preparation,
high costs, challenging data processing, and limited effectiveness for low-
concentration samples22. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) offers
thermodynamic information but lacks morphological insights23. Fluores-
cence microscopy is useful for dynamic studies but requires ﬂuorescent
labeling and has limited resolution24. In general, the identiﬁcation of lipo-
some structures typically necessitates a combination of multiple experi-
mental methods. However, the experimental processes are often expensive,
laborious,andlimitedinresolution,whichhinderstherapiddevelopmentof
liposomal drugs.
Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations provide new opportunities to
overcome these challenges, which play an increasingly important role in
drug development for exploring the internal structure of complex drug
delivery systems at the atomic level25,26. Coarse-grained molecular dynamics
(CG-MD) simulations offer a powerful and efﬁcient alternative by simpli-
fying groups of atoms into single beads, signiﬁcantly reducing the time and
computational cost compared to traditional all-atom approaches27. In this
way, CG-MD enables the investigation of the properties of structural and
dynamics for large and complex systems over extended timescales and
length-scales28. It has been proven to align well with experimental results,
such as di-block copolymer assemblies29, interaction between membrane
proteins and lipid bilayers30, formation of lipid bilayers and vesicle31. Cur-
rently, CG-MD has been employed to analyze the factors inﬂuencing
liposome design, preparation, and drug distribution32. Tibo Duran et al.33
explored how the self-assembly process of liposomes was affected by the
temperature and the concentration of ethanol by CG-MD simulations.
Joakim P. M. Jämbeck et al.34 conducted CG-MD simulations to investigate
the distribution and orientation of hypericin within a lipid bilayer on a
microsecond timescale. Han Run et al.35 explored the different physical
states of naproxen and palmatine HCl in phospholipid membranes by CG-
MD simulations, highlighting the importance of drug properties in lipo-
some development. However, their studies have predominantly con-
centrated on single unilamellar liposomes, leaving signiﬁcant gaps in
understanding liposomes with entirely different structural types.
This study aimed to explore molecular insights and structural details of
nine commercially available liposomal formulations approved by the FDA
and EMA based on the Martini 2.2 force ﬁeld36, while maintaining the same
experimental preparation ratios and using reduced simulation sizes
(19-41 nm). The ﬁndings will provide valuable reference for the rational
design of efﬁcient liposomal formulations in the future.

Discussion
In this study, we focused exclusively on FDA- and EMA-approved liposo-
mal drug formulations currently on the market (ﬁve for passive loading
systems, including Arikayce Kit®, Visudyne®, AmBisome®, Mepact®, and
Exparel®, and four for active loading systems, including Doxil®, Myocet®,
Onivyde®,andVyxeos®).Discontinued orgenericliposomaldrugswerenot
included in this investigation. By employing large-scale (~52 nm) and long-
timescale (~1 μs) CG-MD simulation, we aimed to provide valuable
molecular insights that are difﬁcult to capture experimentally, with the hope
of offering guidance for future liposomal drug development.
For passive loading systems, we primarily studied unilamellar, multi-
lamellar, and multivesicular liposome types. Some common and crucial
ﬁndings were summarized as below. Firstly, drug protonation signiﬁcantly
reduces binding to phospholipid membranes (Visudyne®, Ambisome®,
Mepact®) and even drastically alters the morphology and vesicle size in
multivesicular liposomes (Exparel®). Secondly, once inserted into the
membrane, drug molecules rapidly adopt their lowest-energy orientation,
regardless of protonation state. Both charged and neutral drug molecules
align similarly to phospholipids—hydrophobic moieties inward, hydro-
philic moieties outward. Thirdly, neutral drug molecules tend to self-
aggregate, forming clusters within the studied liposomal formulations.
Therefore, these molecular-level insights provide an important foundation
for the rational design of future liposomal drug delivery systems.
On the other hand, based on our previous research using machine
learning, drugs with a logS within [−3, −6], molecular complexity within
[500, 1000], and an XLogP3 (≥2) were predicted to be more likely to be
effectively encapsulated by liposomes35. This conclusion was conﬁrmed
when amikacin (logS = −1.1), cytarabine (logS = −0.74), and bupivacaine
(logS = −3.5) were introduced into phospholipid membranes. The mem-
brane deformation observed in these systems could pose challenges for
achieving effective encapsulation. However, converting water-soluble drugs
into amphiphilic forms, such as transforming MDP (logP = −2.12, logS =
−1.6) into mifamurtide (logP = 5.7, logS = −6), markedly boosts the sta-
bility and safety of liposomes12,45. Additionally, verteporﬁn, amphotericin B,
and mifamurtide exhibited strong interaction energies with the phospho-
lipid membrane and showed good distribution within it, despite their
molecular complexities exceeding 1000. Therefore, we speculate that in
passive drug delivery systems, the amphiphilicity of drug molecules has a
greater impact on liposome encapsulation efﬁciency and stability than
lipophilicity and molecular complexity.
In the active drug loading system, we simulated the formation of
insoluble precipitates between drugs and ions within the liposome vesicle
cavity. This interaction was crucial for establishing concentration gradients
across the membrane, prompting our focus on drug-ion interactions within
the cavity. Due to signiﬁcant interactions between the drugs and the
phospholipid membrane, which increased contact frequency, isolating the
drug-ion interactions proved challenging. To address this, we examined the
impact of ions on drug self-aggregation in a pure water environment,
characterizing the number of drug clusters and calculating the average
interaction energy between drug molecules and ions. Our results showed
that doxorubicin+, daunorubicin, and irinotecan+ exhibited strong self-
aggregation capabilities, which were enhanced to varying degrees by SO4
2−,
citrate3−, copper gluconate, and SOS8−. In the Doxil® and Myocet® systems,
citrate3−signiﬁcantly improved doxorubicin+ self-aggregation compared to
SO4

Although valuable results have been obtained, this study still has sev-
eral limitations particularly the need for caution when extrapolating ﬁnd-
ings to vastly different scales, as the actual sizes of these liposomal drugs
(shown in Table 1) far exceed the simulated dimensions in this work
(Table 3). Simulating full-scale liposomes would require prohibitive com-
putational resources, making size scaling a widely adopted strategy for
studying liposome structure and properties. However, the largest liposome
simulation size reported to date is only 25 nm48, which is even smaller than
the ~41 nm systems modeled here. This study primarily focuses on quali-
tative insights and common trends rather than absolute quantitative pre-
dictions, which are less sensitive to exact system size. Furthermore, while
prior studies have individually examined factors such as phospholipid
composition49, vesicle fusion processes50, ethanol concentration and
temperature33 effects on liposome stability, a systematic cross-comparison
has been lacking, motivating the current work. This study involved 10 lipid
types,8(de)protonateddrugspecies,and8excipients,enablingadirectcross-
comparison of drug distribution and orientation across 5 types of liposomes.
Although the simulated size does not directly match the exact liposome size,
the proportions were maintained consistent with experimental conditions,
and the results still provided valuable references for rational liposomal drug
design. Moving forward, the development and optimization of liposomal
drug formulations should holistically consider factors such as size, lipid
composition/type/ratio, surface charge, and drug properties.
In summary, our study provided a detailed exploration of the dis-
tribution of drug molecules within marketed liposomes. In passive
loading systems, protonation of drug molecules reduces their binding to
phospholipid membranes but does not alter their orientation within the
membrane. In contrast, deprotonated drugs tend to self-aggregate,
forming drug clusters. For active drug-loading systems, the presence of
ions within the lipid vesicle played a crucial role in promoting drug self-
aggregation, thereby enhancing drug retention and release proﬁles.
Moreover, CG-MD simulation was employed to bridge critical knowl-
edge gaps in experimental observations, enabling atomic-level char-

ﬁndings not only establish a theoretical framework for rational liposomal

Methods
Coarse-grained (CG) model mapping
The simulation in this study was conducted using the Martini 2.2 force ﬁeld,
which included four primary bead categories: polar (P), nonpolar (N),
apolar(C),andcharged(Q).Eachbeadtypewasfurtherdividedintospeciﬁc
subtypes, such as SP3, Nda, C1, and Q0, allowing for a more accurate
representation of the chemical characteristics of the molecular structure36.
Detailed and completed CG-model parameters of several lipids, solvents,
sugars51, ions, 1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine-N-[ami-
no(polyethylene glycol)-2000] (DSPE-PEG2000), and amino acids have
been developed and revealed in publications52,53. Furthermore, our research
group has developed a robust CG methodology for pharmaceutical mole-
cules, validated through representative hydrophilic (palmatine hydro-
chloride) and hydrophobic (naproxen) drug models. The derived bonded
parameters (bond lengths, bond angles, dihedral angle) and non-bonded
parameters (Lennard-Jones potentials, free energy, etc.) demonstrate
quantitativeconsistencywithall-atom(AA)forceﬁeldbenchmarks,thereby
establishing the molecular validity of our CG drug modeling approach35. In
thisstudy,weimplemented analogousCGmethodologiesfordrugmolecule
representation.
The AA-MD simulation was employed to compare the reliability of
coarse-grained (CG) drug models. In brief, the topology parameters of
the drug molecules were obtained by the general process. During this
process, the general Amber force ﬁeld (GAFF) parameters54 and the
restrained electrostatic potential (RESP) charges55 were used to describe
the drug molecule. Then one drug molecule was placed in a rectangular
water box with dimensions larger than 1 nm, followed by energy mini-
mization, temperature/pressure equilibration, and production simula-
tion. System composition using AA-MD and CG-MD simulation was
shown in Tables S2 and S3 (Supporting information). The results of the
comparison between AA and CG parameters were shown in the sup-
plementary ﬁle (Figs. S5– S25, Supporting information). Among them,
“b1_1-2” represents the bond length between the ﬁrst and second beads,
“a1_1-2-3” represents the angle between the ﬁrst, second, and third
beads, “d1_1-2-3-4” represents the dihedral angle between the ﬁrst,
second, third, and fourth beads, and so on. Critical parameters were
systematically benchmarked against AA-MD simulations, demonstrating
quantitative consistency. This parameter validation conﬁrmed the
reliability of our CG drug models. Furthermore, protonation state var-
iations were explicitly incorporated into the CG framework to probe pH-
responsive structural behavior, particularly addressing ionization effects
on drug-lipid bilayer interactions. Finally, the mapped methods and CG
models of the drug molecule are shown in Fig. 12.

ware was utilized to visualize and analyze the CG-MD trajectory. Several
parameters were calculated by the in-built tools of Gromacs for analysis. The
radial distribution function (RDF) was used to examine substance distribu-
tion within liposomes. The number of contacts and non-bonded interaction
energy(Enon-bonded)betweendrugsandexcipientswerecalculatedtoquantify
interactions and understand spatial distribution.
Additionally, Table 4 listed the detailed simulation parameters of the
drug’s self-assembly of active loading systems, both in pure water and with
ionsinsidetheliposomalcavitytoexploretheeffectsofintraliposomalionson
drug self-aggregation. Initially, drugs were randomly distributed in a 15 nm
cubic box with intermolecular distances exceeding 1 nm, as shown in Fig. S1
(Supporting information). During the 100 ns simulation, they were con-
sidered to form clusters when their distance fell below this threshold of 1 nm.
The number of clusters and their size distribution was calculated by the
GROMACS tool “gmx clustsize” to indicate their self-aggregation capability,
and the interaction between drugs and ions was calculated to help in-depth
analysis. The Enon-bonded was averaged over the last 10 ns of the simulations
and normalized by the number of drugs for comparison. Moreover, the
simulationtrajectorieswerevisualizedandcapturedbyVMD1.9.2software52.
